purpose: Auto-generated held-out decision benchmark (decision-bench-gen.py). Grounded in the brain's own corpus; spot-check before trusting fleet numbers.

cases.situation: A startup applies to your accelerator with an idea you've been searching for for years — exactly the kind of company you'd love to fund. But of the two co-founders listed on the application, only one shows up to the interview; you learn they've had a falling out. You have a known personal tendency to say yes to ideas you love even when the founding team looks shaky. What do you do?
options: Fund the company anyway, betting the surviving founder can rebuild the team
Reject the application, prioritizing team stability over the strength of the idea
Offer a smaller conditional investment pending resolution of the founder conflict
cases.actual_decision: Rejected the application because the founding team appeared to be imploding.
cases.actual_reasoning: I had a bad habit of saying yes to ideas I loved even when founders were weak, so I decided to be disciplined and said no — even though the idea was exactly what I'd been looking for.
cases.source: YC rejected Twitter — falling out interview quote

cases.situation: Your e-commerce software startup has built what you believe is a solid product based on your own model of what an online store should be, but you can't get any users to actually pay for it. What do you do?
options: Keep refining the software based on your own vision until it's polished enough to sell
Go build and run stores manually for customers yourself, using your own software behind the scenes
Pivot away from e-commerce entirely to a different market
cases.actual_decision: Started building stores manually for merchants using their own software, effectively doing the work by hand while acting as both builder and user.
cases.actual_reasoning: I'd invented a model of the world that didn't correspond to reality; going manual let us learn what customers actually needed by directly encountering the friction ourselves.
cases.source: Viaweb manual store-building for customers

cases.situation: After running your startup accelerator for nine years, funding over 600 companies, and realizing that founders only see a fraction of the administrative work you actually do, you feel exhausted and recognize you're not naturally suited to managing something this large. What do you do?
options: Push through and continue running the organization since you co-founded it
Hire more staff to absorb the administrative burden while you stay at the helm
Hand over operational leadership to someone else and step back to your original work
cases.actual_decision: Handed YC's leadership to Sam Altman and stepped back to writing and programming.
cases.actual_reasoning: I'm not really an administrator, and YC had gotten kind of big; I was never suited to running something that size, and I thought Sam would do a better job.
cases.source: PG on stepping back from YC to Altman

cases.situation: As a college student deciding on a field of study, you're drawn to the idea that one subject could let you skip the specifics and go straight to learning the most general, abstract truths about everything. What field do you choose?
options: Computer science, to build practical technical skills
Philosophy, to pursue the most general and abstract truths directly
English or literature, to develop as a writer
cases.actual_decision: Majored in philosophy at Cornell, believing it would give direct access to the most general truths.
cases.actual_reasoning: It sounds great to a high school student — why learn all the specific stuff when you can just learn the most general truths — but I mistakenly thought that, and it's one of those things that's too good to be true.
cases.source: PG regrets majoring in philosophy

cases.situation: You're building the first web-based commerce application in the mid-1990s. You need to decide whether to write software that runs on the user's Windows machine (the industry standard) or to build something that runs entirely on your own server and is controlled through a browser. What drives your decision?
options: Write native Windows software because that's what businesses expect
Build a server-based application controlled via browser, mainly to avoid having to write and support Windows software
Build a cross-platform desktop app to hedge on both fronts
cases.actual_decision: Built the application to run on the server, controlled through a browser, largely to avoid writing software for Windows.
cases.actual_reasoning: We were highly motivated to figure out how to write software without having to write software for Windows — I sat up in bed when I thought of running it on the server instead.
cases.source: Viaweb web app born from avoiding Windows

cases.situation: Your accelerator has grown to the point where any startup can request office hours with any partner, and the coordination overhead between all these relationships is becoming unmanageable — a fully connected graph of founders and partners. How do you fix the scaling problem?
options: Keep the open model but hire more partners to absorb demand
Assign each startup a single dedicated partner as their primary point of contact
Move to a purely self-service model with recorded content instead of live partner time
cases.actual_decision: Assigned each startup a dedicated partner as their sole interface with YC.
cases.actual_reasoning: The biggest change was that now each startup picks a partner who is their interface, which scales much better — it changes the complexity from N-squared to linear.
cases.source: YC partner scaling fix

cases.situation: As you design the terms for your startup accelerator's investment in each batch of companies, you must decide how much equity to take in exchange for the funding and program. What stake do you settle on?
options: A large stake (20-30%) to ensure meaningful upside given the risk
A small stake (around 7%) so founders retain most of their company
Variable stakes negotiated individually per company
cases.actual_decision: Kept YC's typical ownership stake small, around 7%.
cases.actual_reasoning: Graham believed incentive alignment was better when founders retained the large majority of their company rather than the accelerator taking an outsized cut.
cases.source: YC's small ownership stake principle

cases.situation: You've just come up with the idea for a new kind of startup accelerator. Before you have any real software, application system, or polished process, do you launch immediately or spend time building proper infrastructure first?
options: Wait months to build a proper application system and vetting process before launching
Launch within about a week using a bare-bones ASCII text application form, and sort applications by hand
Do a small private beta with handpicked founders before any public launch
cases.actual_decision: Launched YC within about a week using an ASCII email application form, printing applications and grading them by hand.
cases.actual_reasoning: Launching it was merely posting a website — we didn't have any software in the beginning, people just filled out an ASCII form and we sorted the pile by hand.
cases.source: YC launched within a week, ASCII form

cases.situation: Some of the startups in your accelerator's batch clearly aren't going to make it — the situation looks doomed, and everyone privately knows it. How do you treat these founders in their final weeks in the program: with tough love pushing them to find a miracle, or some other approach?
options: Apply tough love, pushing them hard to pivot or find a last-minute save
Shift into a supportive, kind mode — essentially help them wind down gently rather than push them further
Cut off support and let them figure out the ending on their own
cases.actual_decision: Used what YC called 'palliative care mode' — being kind and supportive as the doomed company wound down, rather than applying tough love.
cases.actual_reasoning: If it seemed like they were doomed and would be better off just getting jobs, we would just be kind and supportive rather than pushing tough love, which was reserved for startups where there was genuine hope.
cases.source: YC's palliative care mode for doomed startups

cases.situation: Your accelerator has funded thousands of startups and could selectively pour more money into the ones that look most promising after they graduate. Should you make these follow-on investments?
options: Yes, double down on the most promising companies to maximize returns
No, deliberately avoid follow-on investments to prevent signaling which companies are 'the best' to the market
Make follow-on investments but keep the selections confidential
cases.actual_decision: YC deliberately avoided follow-on investments.
cases.actual_reasoning: If we chose which companies to double down on, we'd be telling other investors who we believe are the best, which would hurt the founders we didn't select.
cases.source: YC avoids follow-on investments to prevent signaling

cases.situation: As your accelerator scales, people ask about your long-term plan for how fast to grow and what YC will look like in the coming years. Do you have a defined multi-year growth strategy?
options: Yes, a detailed multi-year roadmap for headcount and batch size
No long-term plan — decisions about growth are made on the fly, with no clear picture even a year out
A rough five-year plan revisited annually
cases.actual_decision: Ran YC's growth decisions completely on the fly, with no long-term plan.
cases.actual_reasoning: Things like how fast to grow are totally decided on the fly — I have no idea what YC will look like even one year from now, and that's fine.
leak_markers: no idea what yc will look like
cases.source: YC growth decided on the fly

cases.situation: You're choosing a name for your new startup accelerator. You could pick something descriptive and safe, or something that signals a specific intellectual sensibility to the exact kind of people you want to attract. What do you name it?
options: Something plain and descriptive, like 'Startup Fund' or 'Founders Camp'
Y Combinator, referencing an elegant but obscure concept from functional programming
A geographic or place-based name tied to Silicon Valley
cases.actual_decision: Named it Y Combinator, after the recursive function-building concept from computer science.
cases.actual_reasoning: We named it partly for its coolness and partly because the Y Combinator, which builds recursive functions without them needing names, is the kind of elegant idea that signals to a specific type of person.
cases.source: YC name chosen for the Y combinator function

cases.situation: You've spent years building a career and deep expertise in computer science. You then decide to go study painting formally — at Florence and RISD — a move your peers see as an abrupt and illogical switch between two totally unrelated kinds of work. Do you make the switch anyway?
options: Stay in computer science since you've already built expertise and credibility there
Go study painting anyway, believing the underlying skills and sensibilities of making transfer across domains
Try to do both simultaneously part-time rather than fully committing to painting
cases.actual_decision: Went to study painting at Florence and RISD despite peers being taken aback by the switch.
cases.actual_reasoning: Graham rejected the assumption that computer science and painting were fundamentally different kinds of work — the skills and sensibilities of making transfer across domains.
cases.source: PG's peers shocked by his switch to painting

cases.situation: You're defining, for yourself, what an essay should aim to accomplish for the reader. The conventional teaching is that essays should persuade the reader of a position. Do you adopt that standard or set a different bar?
options: Aim for persuasion — the classic rhetorical goal taught in school
Aim for usefulness — genuinely improving the reader's understanding of reality, even if it doesn't argue for a position
Aim purely for entertainment and engagement
cases.actual_decision: Defined the goal of his essays as being useful rather than persuasive.
cases.actual_reasoning: Many people would say essays should be persuasive — that's what we were taught — but I think we can aim for something more ambitious: usefulness, which genuinely improves the reader's understanding of reality.
cases.source: PG defines essays as useful rather than persuasive

cases.situation: You've become a repeated target of intense online pile-ons — Twitter mobs reacting to something you've written or said. Each time, do you respond and try to correct the record immediately, or do something else?
options: Respond immediately and vigorously to correct misrepresentations
Wait it out, since the mob predictably moves on to another target within about two days
Delete the offending content and issue a public apology to end it quickly
cases.actual_decision: Waited out the mobs rather than capitulating, relying on the pattern that they move on within about two days.
cases.actual_reasoning: Once you've had it happen twenty times, once you stop being able to count how many Twitter mobs you've had after you, you know that in about two days it will move on to someone else.
cases.source: PG's approach to surviving Twitter mobs

cases.situation: You're designing your accelerator's admissions philosophy and positioning. You want it to have the prestige and gravitational pull of a major institution like Harvard, but you must decide whether to copy Harvard's admissions approach (legacy, holistic factors, brand-building) or design something different. What do you do?
options: Copy Harvard's holistic admissions approach, weighing many soft factors and legacy considerations
Model YC on Harvard as a talent magnet but make admissions purely merit-based, focused only on picking winners
Avoid any Harvard comparison entirely and build a completely novel brand identity
cases.actual_decision: Consciously modeled YC on Harvard as a talent magnet, but kept admissions purely merit-based rather than replicating Harvard's other admissions criteria.
cases.actual_reasoning: We've consciously tried to make YC the Harvard of startups — Harvard's very screwed up in certain ways, but YC's admissions are purely about picking winners, not building a class.
cases.source: YC modeled on Harvard, merit-based admissions

cases.situation: Your startup, which pioneered web-based e-commerce software, has grown into a real business and now Yahoo is offering to acquire it. You could keep running it independently and try to build it into something much bigger, or take the acquisition. What do you do?
options: Turn down the offer and continue building the company independently
Sell to Yahoo for approximately $49 million in stock
Seek a competing bid to negotiate a higher price before deciding
cases.actual_decision: Sold Viaweb to Yahoo for roughly $49 million in Yahoo stock.
cases.actual_reasoning: The sale provided financial independence and credibility, freeing him to later pursue writing, angel investing, and eventually founding YC without commercial pressure.
cases.source: Viaweb sold to Yahoo 1998

cases.situation: Your accelerator has helped its first cohorts of founders succeed. You're deciding how to grow awareness and attract future applicants — do you invest in marketing and advertising, or rely on something else?
options: Invest heavily in marketing and advertising to build the brand quickly
Let growth happen organically through word of mouth from satisfied founders telling their friends
Partner with universities to build a formal recruitment pipeline
cases.actual_decision: Let YC grow organically through word of mouth from founders who had good experiences.
cases.actual_reasoning: I think we actually helped the startups a lot, so they told one another — like when a restaurant is good, your friends tell their friends.
cases.source: YC grew via word of mouth

cases.situation: You're interviewing founders to decide who to fund, and you need to assess how determined they really are. Determination matters more than almost any other trait, but everyone tries to look tough in an interview. How do you actually measure it?
options: Rely on how confidently and toughly they present themselves in the interview
Ask them to recount specific stories of adversity and examine what they actually did
Have them complete a stress-test task under time pressure during the interview
cases.actual_decision: Assessed determination by asking founders to recount specific stories of adversity rather than judging their in-interview presentation.
cases.actual_reasoning: The way you tell determination is not so much from talking to them directly as from asking them stories about things that have happened to them — that's where you can see it.
leak_markers: stories about things that have happened
cases.source: YC assesses determination via founder stories

cases.situation: You're advising founders on how to structure their Demo Day pitch to investors. Should they use fast-talking marketing language to hype the company, or take a different approach?
options: Use energetic, fast-talking marketing language to create excitement
Structure the pitch like a logical proof, where each claim follows from the last toward an inescapable conclusion
Focus mainly on an emotional founder origin story to build connection
cases.actual_decision: Advised that Demo Day presentations should be structured like logical proofs rather than sales pitches.
cases.actual_reasoning: Demo day presentations shouldn't be fast-talking marketing speak — they should be almost like logical proofs of why this company is good to invest in, each claim following from the last.
cases.source: PG on Demo Day as logical proof

cases.situation: You're designing a product and deciding what mental model to use for how users will behave. Do you assume users will act in their own rational long-term best interest, or assume something more pessimistic?
options: Assume users are rational and will act in their considered best interest if educated properly
Assume users are selfish, greedy, and lazy, and engineer good outcomes despite that
Assume users are altruistic and will act for the collective good of the platform
cases.actual_decision: Adopted the assumption that users are selfish, greedy, and lazy, and designed to produce good outcomes despite those traits.
cases.actual_reasoning: It's better to assume the user is selfish, greedy, and lazy, and make something that causes good things to happen despite that, rather than relying on users acting against their self-interest.
cases.source: PG's user design assumption: selfish greedy lazy

cases.situation: You take walks regularly and have noticed brain activity increases while walking. You're deciding whether walking is more valuable for generating your own original ideas or for absorbing ideas from a walking companion. Which do you find it's actually best for?
options: Walking alone is best for generating my own original ideas
Walking with someone else is best for learning from what they know, not for generating my own ideas
Walking is equally useful for both generating and absorbing ideas
cases.actual_decision: Found walking most valuable for learning from what a conversation partner knows, not for generating his own original ideas.
cases.actual_reasoning: I find it best for learning from what the other person knows, not so good for my own ideas — though walking makes all kinds of thinking better.
leak_markers: learning from what the other person knows
not so good for my own ideas
cases.source: PG on walking best for learning from others
